We study this on a real enterprise text-to-SQL engagement: a simulated customer, grounded in the real use case's requirements, starts with an ambiguous request. An agent must discover acceptance criteria, data permissions, and hardware constraints in the discovery phase, then plan and execute a post-training recipe in the delivery phase. Across 15 models, the strongest discover over 80% of withheld requirements and open-weight models discover 40-50%; in the delivery phase, only 25% of runs across eight coding-agent configurations pass all acceptance criteria. We identify four bottlenecks in this engagement: (1) incomplete discovery, with 40% of withheld requirements missing or misrepresented; (2) unreliable execution; (3) underused compute budgets and a lack of systematic comparisons across base models and post-training methods; and (4) benchmark accuracy does not guarantee production readiness. We suggest human review of discovered requirements, monitoring of the agent's plan during execution, and an explicit experiment-environment specification covering hardware, budget scope, and production checks.

title: Disposable Implementations: What Is Software Engineering For?
abstract: Existing implementations are usually maintained for most of their life and replaced only as an exception. Coding agents may change that. If agents can produce new implementations from requirements, tests, architectural constraints, and operational records that survive replacement, changing a system may no longer require modifying its existing codebase. We call this process regeneration. An implementation is disposable when regeneration becomes a routine alternative to maintenance. Regenerating and verifying a clean implementation from current requirements and tests may be cheaper than having agents navigate (and potentially compound) existing technical debt, and could eliminate much of that debt. Yet existing code may contain knowledge absent from the preserved artifacts, including safeguards introduced after failures and assumptions that were never documented. A regenerated implementation may pass the available tests and still lose behavior that matters in production. This leaves open how to establish continuity across replacements and whether regeneration reduces maintenance effort or shifts it to the artifacts and processes that support it. We examine these questions through an exploratory review of practitioner literature. Published examples show that agents can replace existing implementations, but do not establish that repeated regeneration is safe or economical. If implementations become disposable, what should software engineering preserve?

title: Adversarial Speculative Reasoning Improves Long Horizon Agents
abstract: Speculative decoding has been treated purely as a systems optimization that speeds up large language model decoding without changing the model behavior. Under this view, the growing effort to train better draft models has been focused solely on acceptance rate. We argue that this view does not hold true for long-horizon agent reasoning. Measuring frontier open-weight models on complex agentic tasks with different speculative decoding approaches, we found that numerical noise grows within verification windows, and the draft acceptance results of the thinking process can change the output distribution of the model after 30 steps, thus noticeably influencing the reasoning accuracy of long-horizon agents in random directions. In this work, we improve the reasoning capability of target models by controlling such noise. While we cannot change the overall token distribution verified by the target model, we can encode critical reasoning with highest precision by training the draft model to be rejected. We identify these points in agent traces and train the draft model to favor adversarial preference. At inference the trained draft and the target part ways precisely at these decision points, verification restarts, so that critical thinking tokens are sampled from the target model and encoded under its least noisy conditions. This approach makes critical reasoning better indexed and more durable over a long horizon. On complex agentic coding benchmarks, our approach raises end-to-end success rate with no change to the target model or its output distribution. Our results recast the speculative decoding mechanism from a pure accelerator into an active allocator for context precision that improves the accuracy of long-horizon agents by training 0.06% to 0.28% of hosted parameters.

title: Construct Validity of Coding Benchmarks for LLM-based Agentic Coding Tools
abstract: Software developers increasingly adopt LLM-based agentic coding tools to assist them with development tasks. To provide developers with up-to-date information on these tools' effectiveness, prior work introduced benchmarks that enable comparisons across tools. Despite the widespread adoption of such benchmarks, however, recent work has shown that they suffer from issues threatening their validity. Aims. In this work, we aim to complement prior work by analyzing the construct validity of agentic coding benchmarks. Methodology. We analyze nine benchmarks commonly used to evaluate the effectiveness of agentic coding tools. We identify the constructs that the benchmarks claim to measure, the metrics used to operationalize them, and potential confounders that interfere with the measurement. Results. Our findings show that benchmarks commonly operationalize broad concepts such as coding capability with only a small set of metrics. The reported attributes that might confound the measurements vary between benchmarks, indicating a lack of standardization. Conclusions. We conclude with recommendations to strengthen construct validity in agentic coding benchmarks and encourage further empirical work to better understand the effectiveness of agentic coding tools.

title: PersonaCodeBench: Evaluating Coding Agents in Persona-driven Human-Interactive Sessions
abstract: Coding agents must deliver correct software while respecting users' expertise, preferences, and working conditions. Existing benchmarks increasingly incorporate interaction, yet personalized requirement fulfillment remains underexplored. We introduce PersonaCodeBench, which turns user characteristics into verifiable obligations in persona-driven multi-turn coding sessions. Our persona pool spans roles, technical abilities, interaction preferences, and practical constraints, yielding task-grounded evolved requirements for implementation, permissions, testing, explanation, and delivery. At runtime, a controller governs user simulator responses and requirement disclosure, using online requirement evaluation to provide feedback and advance the interaction. Requirements emerge progressively, with their content, disclosure conditions, and acceptance criteria fixed before evaluation. A completion verifier and a personalization verifier separately assess native correctness and persona fulfillment. Joint pass requires both adherence to the declared budget and compliance with validity conditions. We evaluate all major frontier agents, establish a comprehensive leaderboard, and conduct detailed experimental analyses to validate effectiveness. PersonaCodeBench supports reproducible evaluation of coding agents' ability to meet explicit, personalized user expectations alongside coding objectives.

title: SWEOps-Bench: Evaluating Agents for End-to-End Resolution of Software-Induced Cloud Incidents
abstract: As autonomous agents advance, the traditional boundary between software development and cloud operations gradually blurs, increasing the need for integrated incident detection, localization, and remediation. Existing benchmarks evaluate isolated diagnostic queries or repository-level program repair, failing to test continuous incident resolution across operational clusters and source repositories. We introduce SWEOps-Bench, an interactive benchmark comprising 55 reproducible incident tasks derived from confirmed historical defects across 16 Kubernetes operator projects. Each task preserves the original software repository and initializes in a healthy cluster before a controlled workload triggers the historical fault. Agents investigate runtime evidence and submit source or configuration repairs through a terminal interface, while the harness builds and deploys the changes within a shared time budget. Evaluation covers stage-wise accuracy, verified recovery, penalized lifecycle latency, and token consumption. Across six agent-model configurations, faulty-state detection ranges from 72.7% to 90.9%, whereas overall recovery ranges from only 14.5% to 52.7%, exposing a substantial gap between recognizing incidents and resolving them end to end. Trajectory analysis further shows that reported diagnosis and final recovery only partially coincide: some tasks achieve verified recovery despite an incorrect reported RCA, while runtime symptom clearance can still fail fix-specific functional verification. SWEOps-Bench establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluating autonomous agents in integrated development and operational environments.

title: A.S.E 2.0: Understanding How Repository Context Impacts the Security of LLM-Generated Code
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding assistants and agents construct a repository context before generating code. For security-sensitive code, this context decides whether the model sees the project's safeguards (e.g., authorization checks) or insecure code to imitate. However, context construction is designed almost exclusively for functional correctness, and secure-code benchmarks treat the context as fixed, so how repository context affects the security of generated code remains unclear. We construct CASE-Bench, a benchmark of 145 repository-level tasks from real CVEs in 51 projects. Each task runs in Docker, has functional tests and a proof-of-concept exploit validated in both directions, and is annotated with the repository code that enforces or undermines its security. Using CASE-Bench, we compare 13 context construction methods and six controls with six LLMs, edit single context elements, and analyze coding-agent trajectories. We find that (1) functionality-oriented context raises the functional pass rate by up to 8.2 percentage points (pp) but the secure pass rate by at most 3.7 pp, (2) withholding a safeguard lowers the secure pass rate by up to 8.1 pp, while one inserted insecure exemplar raises correct-but-exploitable code by 6.3 pp, and (3) coding agents observe the relevant safeguard in only 27-36% of trajectories. These findings inform security-aware context construction and secure-code evaluation.

title: Trace2Eval: Contextualized Evaluation of Coding Agents from Real-World Traces
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly used in real-world workflows across diverse domains, motivating evaluation grounded in real user tasks. Existing benchmarks, however, largely rely on static public tasks with reference patches or hidden tests. Next-generation coding-agent benchmarks should therefore move beyond correctness on fixed tasks toward continually renewed evaluation of overall artifact quality in real user workflows. We propose Trace2Eval, a dynamically updatable pipeline that constructs benchmarks from real-world interaction trajectories. Trace2Eval employs a multi-agent reconstruction system to analyze the filtered trajectory, recover the original user query, restore the workspace files to their pre-interaction state, and rebuild a trajectory-equivalent execution environment. A candidate agent then executes the reconstructed query to produce an initial artifact. To evaluate these artifacts, the pipeline iteratively refines human rubrics through inter-annotator alignment, and calibrates judge agents against human assessments using source-code and runtime evidence. Guided by feedback from the Trace2Eval pipeline, models revise their initial artifacts, yielding a mean score gain of 10.05 percentage points across 19 model-harness configurations and a maximum of 19.28 percentage points for DeepSeek-V4-Pro with Claude Code, which supports rubric feedback as actionable guidance for artifact improvement.

title: ServerBench: How can your coding agents design specialized LLM serving systems?
abstract: Large language model (LLM) coding agents develop software through experimentation, offering an opportunity to design the serving systems supporting their own operation. Effective serving requires coordinating implementation and operating decisions under session dependencies, latency constraints, and correctness requirements. We introduce ServerBench, a benchmark for agentic design of complete, specialized LLM serving systems. Agents experiment against a common objective, dollars per dollar: latency-qualified token value per dollar of GPU cost. Stateful replay preserves session dependencies, and independent verification checks the submitted system. Across 11 coding-agent models and three deployments, Claude Sonnet 5.5 achieves 2.97 dollars per dollar on Gemma E4B, $4.87\times$ the vLLM reference; 22 of 33 runs yield verified systems, and 13 exceed the strongest baseline. Our analysis identifies three findings: high-value designs coordinate capacity improvements with load selection; agents interpret performance feedback through workload-relevant experiments; and reliable delivery requires verification of the execution paths introduced by optimization. Overall, ServerBench supports systematic study of how agents translate service objectives and feedback into effective, verified serving systems for given task specifications.

title: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
abstract: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

title: Multi-step SWE: Can Coding Agents Keep Building on Their Own Code Over Long Horizons?
abstract: Developers rarely give a coding agent a single request: they ask it to build a component and then to extend, upgrade, and optimize it, each time on code the agent itself wrote. Most benchmarks, however, score one task at a time. We introduce Multi-step SWE, a long-horizon benchmark of 69 software engineering tasks, each a chain of 5-15 dependent steps on a single codebase. Every step is a complete, multi-hour engineering request that starts from the code the agent produced in the preceding steps, so early design decisions and errors carry forward. The tasks span four families of engineering work and nine languages, include both from-scratch builds and existing open-source codebases, and ground every step in an existing source of truth that defines both the instruction and its verifier. Across nine frontier models, the strongest model reaches a solve rate of only 18.5%, and 38 of the 69 tasks are not solved by any model. We release Multi-step SWE publicly at https://multistepswe.com.

title: SeVerus: Context-Aware, Gamified Benchmarking for Rust Verification
abstract: Coding agents achieve high success rates on existing benchmarks for Verus, a verifier for Rust programs. These benchmarks typically provide the auxiliary lemmas needed to complete a proof. In practice, however, such lemmas must be discovered and proved. To capture this challenge, we present SEVERUS, a context-aware technique to generate Verus benchmarks that organizes verification tasks into quests, each divided into levelsin a gamified manner. Using the original proof dependencies in verified projects, SEVERUS constructs one quest per verification target and progressively removes proof context to create individual levels. These levels range from the easiest, requiring completing only a single missing lemma, to the hardest, requiring proving the target without any supporting lemmas. An independent checker rejects changes to executable code, weakened specifications, and unsound proof constructs. A noisy binary search estimates the highest level that an agent can solve reliably. Applied to six open-source Verus projects, SEVERUS generates 819 quests comprising 10,095 levels. Experiments with Codex using GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, and with Claude Code using Sonnet 4.6, show that success decreases and cost increases as proof context is withdrawn. The strongest agent solves the final level of 52 of 60 sampled quests, yet can only reliably solve 35% of their levels, with failures concentrated in longer quests. Successful GPT-6 Sol proofs rarely reproduce the withheld lemmas, instead, using alternative proof decompositions. By systematically varying proof context, SEVERUS provides a foundation for constructing verification benchmarks that can continue to challenge increasingly capable coding agents.

title: How Should Agents See Code? Rethinking Code Representations for Agentic Software Engineering
abstract: LLM agents are increasingly used for repository-level software engineering tasks. However, most agents still access repositories through raw files, lexical search, and shell commands, treating code primarily as text. This paper investigates map-based code-representation workflows as a design variable in agentic software engineering, examining how different repository views change agents' retrieval behavior, task success, token use, and latency. In this paper, we study five code-representation workflows: abstract syntax trees, call graphs, module dependencies, documentation-enriched search, and a hybrid workflow that combines them. Each workflow exposes a repository map that the agent can query during a task. We evaluate Claude Code with Haiku 4.5 against a raw-tool baseline on four repository-level tasks: fault localization with LinuxFLBench, repository-level code generation and repair with SWE-bench Pro, test generation with SWT-bench, and security patching with SecBench. The results show that representation workflows are most useful as token-saving tools when localization is the bottleneck, while their success gains narrow when the decisive step is patch or test authoring. On LinuxFLBench, all five workflows improve recall@10 over the baseline (0.757-0.829 vs. 0.717) and reduce token usage by 25-39%. On SWE-bench Pro, resolution remains close to the baseline (44.3-50.6% vs. 49.0%) while token usage drops by 17-26%. On SecBench, Callgraph has the highest patch-resolution rate in this sample (34.3% vs. 28.9%) and uses fewer tokens, but all workflows increase latency. On SWT-bench, Hybrid and Docs have the highest reproducing-test rates in this sample (47.8% and 47.2% vs. 44.7%), but all workflows use more tokens and take longer. Overall, map-based workflows change both what the agent inspects and how much it spends, but their benefits are task-dependent rather than universal.

title: Take It From Here: Evaluating Coding Agents On Project Takeover
abstract: Coding agents increasingly collaborate on long-term projects. When taking over a project, they need to recover currently applicable requirements from the interaction history and update them in response to new requests. However, most coding benchmarks do not include long interaction histories, and some evaluations that consider history still do not cover the full process from requirement reconstruction to project delivery. We therefore provide agents with the interaction history, current request, and pre-request project environment, ask them to make the requested changes, and assess takeover performance through delivery tests. Across six model-harness configurations and 37 targets eligible for executable validation, the mean complete-delivery rate under Full History is only 4.95%. We then use requirement atoms to independently diagnose a larger set of takeover targets, examining relevant information identification, pre-request state reconstruction, and current request processing. We further supply correct pre-request or target states to examine the remaining difficulties in requirement processing and project modification. The diagnostics show that none of the six configurations produces fully correct post-request requirement states, and a case illustrates omission of previously recovered constraints during updating. With correct target states supplied, the mean complete-delivery rate is 8.11%, with build and regression pass rates of 96.40% and 90.99%, but target-test success remains 9.01%. These results show difficulties in both forming target requirement states and implementing supplied targets in existing projects. Based on these findings, we introduce ReqMemBench, which combines requirement diagnostics with delivery validation to support systematic evaluation of project takeover.

title: FINCOSMOS: An Open-World Evaluation Paradigm for Agents in Finance
abstract: Language agents increasingly work for users on the open Web, and finance is where trusting them is hardest. The data must come from the Web, the strategy lives in the user's head, and correctness depends on time, so an agent can fail silently: a strategy the user never asked for, unverified data, or a backtest that uses the future yields a report as convincing as a correct one. Existing benchmarks close the world somewhere, fixing the task, the data, or the timeline, and thereby remove these failures instead of measuring them. We introduce FINCOSMOS, an open-world evaluation paradigm for agents doing financial work. A simulated user holds a hidden strategy sampled from a compositional grammar and reveals it only when asked. The agent receives no data, so it must acquire data from the Web, build its own backtest under a data cutoff, and deliver verifiable results. Grading needs no reference answer. Programs verify point-in-time correctness and recompute every reported metric, the delivered strategy is checked against the hidden specification, and a run is accepted only when the user is satisfied and none of 15 veto checks fails. Across four coding agents and a model without tools in 150 sessions, no session is accepted: every session that the simulated user signed off fails a program check, and agents raise only 54--64\% of the details they were not told. Human experts attribute 88.33\% of failures to the agents. With FINCOSMOS feedback, an agent with persistent memory learned all ten tasks.

title: A Low Similarity Score Does Not Show Independence after Source-Conditioned Repository Rewriting
abstract: Maintainers sometimes cite a low token-similarity score as evidence that an LLM-assisted rewrite of a copyleft project is independent of the original. We test what such a score can support under \emph{source-conditioned} rewriting: a coding agent keeps the original in its working copy, rewrites the repository, and iterates until a fixed behavioural harness passes, with no human edit to the code. On 69 rewrites of six copyleft Python projects we find that: \ding{182}~Agent-only rewriting is inexpensive and often yields low scores. Every controlled rewrite passes the harness after repair, usually within half an hour for the initial rewrite. Under a ground-up rearchitecture prompt, most rewrites fall below 25\% JPlag similarity and still pass the harness. \ding{183}~A single low score is an unreliable witness. Identical project--agent--prompt configurations produce wide spreads in similarity; run-to-run variation dominates project and agent effects, and in more than a third of configurations the three repeats straddle the threshold. Rewrites retain more of the original's imports and fingerprint facts than unrelated projects do, yet hand-written independent implementations of the same task often retain as much, and neither signal separates the two groups better than chance. Thus a low score on one rewrite is weak evidence of independence: another run of the same agent may score high. Claims based on similarity should report repeated generations, and candidate provenance signals should be checked against same task independent implementations, not only against unrelated projects.

title: Create Your Own Work Stack: Deploying Self-hosted AI and Tooling in a Tech Startup
abstract: Self-hosting AI is often presented as a way to reduce inference costs and increase control, but deployment introduces its own costs. We report our experience deploying a hybrid AI stack at Grayhat Developers, a small software company with an AI-intensive development workflow. Our initial motivation was to counter the growing cost of commercial AI usage: Claude/Codex incurred approximately \$325 per month, with more than 25.93 billion recorded tokens. We experimented with local open-source models as replacements for commercial coding agents, but after learning that their performance and inference speed were insufficient, we adopted a hybrid approach in which commercial agents remained responsible for complex tasks while local models handled lower-complexity tasks, organizational information retrieval, and synchronization with self-hosted tools including Outline, Plane, and ERPNext. We estimated that approximately 30--40\% of our commercial AI workload was associated with context transfer, documentation synchronization, task management, and related operational coordination. By moving this work to local models, we estimate that approximately 90\% of this coordination workload could be handled without commercial inference, corresponding to an estimated 27--36\% reduction in overall commercial-AI workload or cost-equivalent usage. Our first internal deployment nevertheless failed to achieve adoption because it introduced UX friction. Replacing it with a centrally configured deployment substantially improved feedback and adoption. We conclude that local inference is most useful not as a wholesale replacement for commercial AI, but as part of a hybrid architecture that assigns tasks according to their capability requirements, cost, context demands, and operational sensitivity.

title: Hard Issue, Weak Model, or Bad Run? Rethinking Failure Prediction for Coding Agents
abstract: Trajectory-based failure predictors for software engineering (SE) agents read the partial trajectory of a run to flag whether it is going right or wrong. If it is going wrong, the run can be stopped, retried, or switched to another model. We ask whether these predictors learn anything about the run itself. On public SWE-bench Verified trajectories, where each model attempts each issue once, two run-independent factors dominate predictor performance. The first is issue difficulty: a reference score that never looks at the run, only at how hard the issue is for other models, reaches 0.92 AUROC, whereas trajectory predictors reach about 0.62. The second is model ability: within an issue, knowing which model ran predicts failure better than our predictors do, and the predictors largely reproduce the overall ability ranking of the models. Beyond difficulty and ability, what predictors gain from the trajectory is statistically equivalent to zero. This confusion carries over to the actions taken after a prediction. Model switching is often motivated by the gap between the best single model's resolution rate and an any-model oracle. This gap is no larger than random variation alone produces. Per-issue switching gains nothing on held-out runs. In a repeated-run pilot, the same model often solves an issue in some runs and fails it in others. Retrying thus has real room to repair failures, but it rescues only failures caused by a bad run, not those on an issue beyond the model's ability. Current predictors cannot tell the causes apart, as they mostly predict the issue and the model, not the run. We call for failure prediction that explains why a run fails, evaluated on repeated-run benchmarks and in closed-loop, equal-budget settings.

title: Learning the Task or Learning the Verifier? Rethinking Criteria Exposure in Embodied Self-Improvement
abstract: Self-improving embodied agents are increasingly being developed and compared on robot simulation benchmarks. Several recent works expose the benchmark's success criteria to the learning agent, a practice we call Criteria Exposure (CE). These criteria, originally written to verify policies trained by imitation learning, often demand more than the corresponding language instructions, so a score from such a verifier may not faithfully reflect whether the instructed task was completed, especially for robot-control programs written by an agent. As embodied coding agents report ever higher benchmark scores, a natural question arises: when a coding agent is exposed to the benchmark's criteria, does it generate code that better performs the instructed task, or code that simply overfits to the verification criteria? We conduct controlled experiments with a self-improving agent with and without CE, and find that with CE the agent quickly produces code with a higher success rate under the given criteria, but this advantage disappears when the criteria are changed slightly without departing from the original instructions. More importantly, the skills the agent develops under CE transfer poorly across tasks. We further propose instruction-faithful criteria and show that they better reflect the performance of agent-generated programs.

title: Benchmarks as Software: Terminal-Bench and the Case for Continuous Benchmarks
abstract: Coding agents are among the most economically consequential deployments of LLMs to date, making reliable evaluation increasingly important. Yet even benchmarks that are carefully validated at release can become stale. As models improve, they can discover valid solutions that existing verifiers reject, while changes to evaluation infrastructure can invalidate assumptions embedded in tasks and tests. We call the resulting accumulation of defects benchmark maintenance debt: a growing gap between benchmark scores and the capabilities they are intended to measure. We introduce a continuous-validation workflow for agentic benchmarks that combines community reports, task artifacts, agent traces, automated oracle checks, and human-gated repairs. We apply this workflow to Terminal-Bench 2.0, a benchmark that underwent extensive human and LM-assisted review and red-teaming before release. Our audit identifies issues in roughly 30% of the benchmark, and we release the resulting repairs as Terminal-Bench 2.1. These repairs change evaluation results: accuracy increased by over 10 percentage points and leaderboard positions move by up to three ranks, even as the overall ranking remains highly correlated (Spearman rho = 0.958). We evaluate how resource allocation shapes benchmark conclusions. We show that fixed wall-clock can materially change agent performance: For example, extending the time limit closes a 20pp harness gap on GPT 5.4 and shrinks a 30 pp gap on GPT 5.4 mini to 5 pp. Benchmark maintenance is therefore not only about repairing task artifacts: resource budgets are part of the measurement specification and must be validated alongside the tasks themselves. More broadly, benchmark maintenance debt is not just accumulated implementation bugs: our results show that as models improve, both evaluation assumptions and resource settings may need to be revalidated.

title: ReproBridge: Building Reproducibility into ML Research Artifacts
abstract: Reproducing machine learning experiments requires reconstructing procedures from information scattered across papers, released code, and supporting artifacts. For coding agents, reproduction success can therefore depend on their ability to fill in missing details, rather than on the released artifacts alone. We ask whether preserving recovered procedures and decisions improves subsequent independent reproduction. We define a standardized artifact design comprising a refined codebase, environment setup, experiment launchers, and a reproduction guide, and introduce ReproBridge, an agent workflow for constructing these refined reproducible artifacts. ReproBridge-Bench provides 1,029 tasks from 387 experiments across 36 papers, anchored by five human-verified reference scores per task. Agents attempt tasks in fresh sessions with raw code or refined artifacts; a separate Auditor checks execution evidence. Across four evaluated models, refined artifacts raise mean reproduction success from 76.4% to 92.6% and reduce downstream API spending by 19.7% on average. The cross-model success-rate spread narrows from 21.6 to 3.9 percentage points, with all four models achieving mean success rates above 90%. Removing any component reduces success in the ablation study, with the largest losses from code and environment removal. These results suggest that preserving execution knowledge helps even models with lower raw-code success reproduce experiments more reliably and at lower API cost.

title: Cognitive Tours: Making Understanding a Deliverable in AI-Assisted Development
abstract: Generative AI and agentic coding are accelerating software development, leading to concerns about technical debt. But two less visible forms of debt, cognitive debt and intent debt, are emerging as key risks to software health. Cognitive debt is the absence or erosion of a team's shared understanding where no one can confidently explain how a system works or predict the impact of a change. Intent debt is the lack of clearly articulated goals, constraints, and rationale that explain what the system is for and guide how it should evolve. This paper presents Cognitive Tours, a tool designed to mitigate and repair cognitive and intent debt. Cognitive Tours is a web-based prototype for creating and following curated paths connecting user needs, design decisions, code, tests, and open questions. AI-assisted skills help audit existing waypoints and tours for possible problems or staleness and suggest candidates for new ones; humans decide what matters, verify relationships, and construct the narrative. This division of work deliberately preserves productive friction: the sensemaking involved in selecting, explaining, and revising a tour, which is intended to foster and share understanding. Our demonstration uses a tour of Cognitive Tours itself to introduce the tool and illustrate its design decisions and interaction mechanisms. A proposed evaluation agenda concludes the paper. A demo is available at https://cognitive-tours-demo.vercel.app/

title: Divide, Diagnose, and Compose: Optimizing Agentic Pipelines and Harnesses
abstract: Building agentic pipelines that achieve high task performance while keeping cost and latency low requires jointly optimizing heterogeneous and coupled design choices, including prompts, topology, model selection, and tool policies. Manually searching this combinatorial design space is expensive and time-consuming, while existing automated optimizers typically operate within a predefined subset of this space, modify the pipeline monolithically, or provide little structured evidence for pipeline changes. To mitigate these challenges, we introduce the Decomposed Credit-Assignment Framework (DeCAF), which adapts the design space to the given benchmark and pipeline, optimizes each dimension separately, and generates reasoning traces for every decision. Given a task specification, benchmark examples, and a seed pipeline, DeCAF identifies relevant optimization dimensions and generates diverse experimental hypotheses for each. Independent coding-agent sessions then optimize each dimension under a restricted edit scope, jointly evaluating performance, inference cost, and latency while recording all hypotheses, edits, and outcomes of each experiment. A final synthesis session combines compatible findings across all dimensions and uses a component-level trajectory evaluator, which derives role-specific rubrics from each agent's instructions, to localize underperforming components and guide cross-dimension revisions. Across a diverse suite of agentic benchmarks, DeCAF improves average task performance by 2.58 percentage points, while reducing inference cost by 4.30% and end-to-end latency by 42.45% compared to the best overall baseline.

title: Frontier3DBench: Benchmarking Coding Agents for 3D Creation across Objects, Scenes, and Interactive Open Worlds
abstract: Coding agents combine visual understanding with program execution, offering a new route to automated 3D creation. By translating images and instructions into editable programs, they bring reconstruction, generation, and editing into a shared workflow. Yet existing benchmarks fragment evaluation across task scopes and protocols, leaving their capabilities across construction levels unclear. We propose Frontier3DBench, a unified benchmark of 145 tasks across 9 categories spanning object, scene, and interactive open-world creation, with joint evaluation of appearance, structure, and behavior. Experiments with 11 model-harness configurations reveal strengths that vary by level: GPT-6.1-sol leads the object and scene levels and achieves the highest overall score of 66.02/100, whereas GPT-6-astra leads interactive world construction. However, all configurations score lower on reference reconstruction than on text-driven generation in object and scene tasks. Producing plausible content thus remains easier than reproducing specified geometry, layouts, and visual details. Moreover, generated worlds average 83.08/100 on local mechanisms but only 20.82 on motion clearance and 30.26 on stateful workflows: individual mechanisms often function, whereas complete activities that require coordinated actions and persistent state remain difficult. These results identify reference fidelity and coordinated activity completion as central bottlenecks for coding agents in 3D creation.

title: Deliberate Pacing for Human Oversight in Agentic Software Development
abstract: Agentic AI increasingly enables software development activities to proceed without continuous human involvement. While this autonomy may accelerate development, it also raises questions about when developers can meaningfully oversee software development done by agents. We propose deliberate pacing: intentionally adjusting when and how autonomous development proceeds to preserve opportunities for meaningful oversight. Drawing on an exploratory multivocal literature review of 20 sources, we identify three factors motivating this vision: changing relative costs of human involvement, the timing of oversight opportunities, and interdependencies between pacing decisions across the software development life cycle. We argue that neither uninterrupted autonomy nor frequent human intervention is universal. Instead, pacing should balance opportunities to understand and influence consequential decisions against costs in human attention, development time, and rework. We outline a research agenda to investigate when deliberate pacing is beneficial, how intervention timing affects oversight, and how pacing decisions interact across development activities.

title: AnimWeb-Bench: Benchmarking Animated Webpage Code Generation from Videos
abstract: Animation is pervasive on the Web, the CSS animation property alone appears on over three-quarters of webpages. Yet existing webpage code generation benchmarks target static screenshots, user-triggered interactions, or isolated motion graphics, leaving the ability of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) and coding agents to reconstruct complete animated webpages largely unexplored. To fill this gap, we introduce AnimWeb-Bench, the first benchmark for animated webpage code generation from videos. It comprises 124 real-world webpages spanning 7 application domains and 33 animation types, with 91.9% of pages combining multiple types, each paired with a reference video and the static assets of the original webpage. We further propose a human-aligned, two-dimensional evaluation protocol: Static Appearance Fidelity measures structure, text, color, and visual similarity on aligned keyframes, while Animation Fidelity tracks UI components across frames and compares their position, size, velocity, and appearance with those in the reference video. Evaluating 14 MLLMs and three coding agents reveals: (1) reproducing webpage animations is substantially more difficult than reproducing static appearance; (2) explicit frame inspection and render feedback improve the reconstruction quality of coding agents; and (3) rapid, continuous changes are harder to reproduce than discrete state transitions. Our code and dataset are available at https://starry1001.github.io/AnimWeb-Bench-website/ .

title: REINS: A Self-Evolving Agent Harness for Real-Time Trajectory Planning
abstract: Agent harnesses -- runtime scaffolds that wrap an LLM's reasoning loop with tool dispatch, verification, and persistent memory -- have become the standard substrate for deploying LLMs as autonomous agents, as demonstrated by Claude Code and Codex in software engineering. In trajectory planning, however, this paradigm has not taken hold: existing LLM-based trajectory planning methods either keep the LLM in the decision loop, exceeding the millisecond-level control budget, or offload it to offline rules or training-time supervision -- leaving the runtime planner non-evolving. Intermediate hybrids still lack the verification-and-consolidation loop that makes harnesses reliable. We ask: what runtime harness would let an LLM planner meet real-time constraints while self-evolving into a deployable one? We propose REINS, a harness built on three LLM-planner couplings: LLM outputs are (i) grounded to a learned variable-level dynamics model, (ii) verified via calibrated predicates and forward rollout, and (iii) consolidated into an indexed rule memory that serves future scenes in O(log n) without re-invoking the LLM. The harness closes a self-evolution loop: familiar scenes resolve by memory lookup; novel scenes invoke the LLM, whose verified outputs enrich the memory. Without modifying LLM weights, REINS attains 98%+ compliance, nearly 50% collision reduction, and 1.9-4.6 ms latency on simulated and real-world benchmarks at the tactical decision layer, with LLM invocation rate monotonically declining as memory matures. Code: https://github.com/ZhihongCui/REINS

title: Patch correctness in automated program repair: A five-dimensional evidence framework and cross-benchmark audit from classical repair to coding agents
abstract: Tests guide automated program repair and determine which candidate patches are reported as successful. Repository-level coding agents extend this feedback loop by generating tests and revising code after observing execution results. This technical report introduces a five-dimensional evidence profile and reporting protocol to audit how test observations support patch-correctness claims across classical repair systems and coding agents. We assemble an audit dataset of 39 benchmark and evaluation artifacts: 32 primary empirical studies, one institutional technical audit, and six prior taxonomic baselines. We code the 33 primary contributions along five dimensions: test provenance and exposure, behavioral scope, oracle basis and dependence, execution integrity, and label adjudication. The central distinction separates checks visible during repair search from evidence reserved for final assessment. Four worked comparative audits show how changed candidate populations, oracle rules, or execution budgets alter reported detection rates. Additional tests can expose missed faults while rejecting valid alternatives or reducing correct-repair yield under a fixed budget. Repository-level audits separate issue reproduction from candidate-patch discrimination and distinguish automated discrepancy detection from requirements-based adjudication. An evidence matrix links each coded decision to supporting passages and records shared benchmark ancestry. We specify a reporting protocol for repair benchmarks and maintenance pipelines that retains uncertain judgments and records validation cost alongside fault detection and valid-patch retention.

title: When Coding Agents Get Arms: Safety Risks Across the Digital-Physical Boundary
abstract: Advances in spatial understanding have enabled frontier models to power coding agents that control a real robot arm zero-shot and end-to-end, without task-specific demonstrations or retraining. This brings two new safety challenges. First, the extensive knowledge of frontier models lets these agents perform tasks that earlier VLA and WAM paradigms could not, opening the door to new forms of capability misuse. Second, coding agents can access digital resources such as web pages and emails. Threats in these resources, such as indirect prompt injection, can carry over into the physical world when the agent controls a robot. We therefore introduce ArmedAgent, the first systematic benchmark to evaluate both risks for coding agents performing zero-shot robot control. It covers robustness, malicious use, and indirect injection across 36 tasks in 5 scenarios, evaluated in simulation and validated on a physical robot arm. A distinctive portion of the tasks target harmful behaviors that earlier VLA paradigms could not perform. Testing several frontier models, including GPT-6-Astra, under widely used agent frameworks, we find substantial safety risks in current systems.

title: Same Error, Different Recovery: How Delivery Changes LLM Agent Behavior
abstract: A tool-using language model must decide whether to retry a failed call, correct it, or stop and tell the user. The error text alone may not be enough: the same feedback can lead to different actions depending on where it appears in the conversation. We isolate this delivery problem by varying placement, guidance, retained history and turn structure. Two studies with plans fixed before data collection, across 13 open models from 3B to 70B parameters, compare the next action and subsequent task completion, with exact deterministic reruns. A new user turn that retains the failed exchange avoids the severe stopping failure observed in Llama models when that exchange is removed. It is non-inferior to history rewriting in pooled synthetic comparisons, but is not best for every model. We implement this form as an opt-in recovery layer within a deterministic inference engine and evaluate it on public benchmarks and a coding agent. On ToolMaze, it raises success on explicit errors by 14.2 points with 7-8B models and 10.5 points with 32-70B models; Loud/Quiet, 24 multi-turn tasks with visible failures and silent corruption, scored by final-state agreement, shows no measurable gain. A client given the exact fault kind performs better still. The findings support delivery as a distinct factor in recovery, not an engine-exclusive solution or a universal retry policy.

title: Silinx: An Open, Browser-Based HDL Design Platform for Teaching Digital Systems on FPGA Boards
abstract: Many digital systems courses teach on FPGA boards whose vendor tool is no longer maintained: the Digilent Basys2 and Nexys2 (Xilinx Spartan-3E) and Nexys3 and Atlys (Spartan-6) need Xilinx ISE 14.7, discontinued since 2013 and hard to install on the computers and tablets students use today. The author presents Silinx, a free (AGPL-3.0) HDL design platform for teaching that keeps ISE's Project Navigator workflow but runs in a web browser with nothing to install. A module can be written in VHDL or Verilog, in C or C++ through Silinx HLS, which is compatible with AMD's Vitis HLS and passes all 73 of its introductory examples, or drawn as a schematic, an ASM chart, a state diagram, a Boolean function with its Karnaugh map, or a Petri net, from which its HDL is generated. Designs are checked with explanations written for beginners, simulated, run on an emulated board, built, and programmed onto a real board over WebUSB. The implementation flow is open and runs in the browser: Yosys and nextpnr compiled to WebAssembly, with Silinx's own device data, timing model and bitstream writer for the Spartan-3E and Spartan-6, built by black-box observation of ISE's documented tools; Lattice iCE40 boards use the existing open iCE40 tools, and further families are planned. ISE is the oracle: Silinx's bitstreams are byte-identical to those ISE writes for the same placed and routed design, and pass ISE's design rule check. Against ISE at the same optimization goal, the open flow uses 15% fewer slices with 14% shorter critical paths when optimizing for area, and 21% fewer slices with 8% shorter critical paths when optimizing for speed (geometric means over 45 open-source designs built by both flows). The author also describes how the platform was developed with AI coding agents under test-first project rules.

title: Repository-Context-Guided Image Understanding for Agentic Software Development
abstract: Coding agents increasingly receive UI screenshots as part of bug reports, yet degraded image quality - caused by low resolution, compression artifacts, or small rendered text - can prevent them from identifying the relevant UI elements and source files. Vision-language models become less reliable as image quality deteriorates, while OCR-assisted approaches may propagate recognition errors from degraded inputs. Both approaches are limited when the visual evidence required for localization is no longer clearly observable in the query screenshot. We propose augmenting coding agents with repository-rendered reference images: crisp screenshots generated from the same codebase that the agent is tasked with modifying. These references provide readable visual evidence of the application's UI while preserving the current, potentially bug-containing implementation state. Because they are generated from the available repository rather than requiring a known bug-free version, they can be produced automatically for reproducible application states without manual image annotation. We evaluate the approach on a controlled benchmark derived from SWE-bench Multimodal by injecting visual UI bugs into a real web application. We vary screenshot degradation and reference-image provision and measure whether the coding agent identifies the correct source file. The results show that reference images improve file localization especially for degraded image quality, increasing the gold file match rate under fourfold downsampling with JPEG compression. We confirmed with further analysis that the proposed approach recognizes text approximately 12 percentage points better than language biased OCR under the same degradation.

title: SWE-Time: Benchmarking Temporal Repository Understanding
abstract: Repository-level code-understanding benchmarks have progressively expanded the spatial scope of reasoning, from local code to entire repositories, while largely treating each repository as a static snapshot. However, how models reason about repository evolution over time remains largely unexplored. We introduce SWE-Time, a benchmark for temporal repository understanding that makes repository evolution itself the reasoning target. SWE-Time evaluates two complementary temporal directions: retrospective understanding of repository evolution through historical regression analysis and prospective understanding of intended changes from pre-change repository states. To enable realistic yet reliable evaluation in these settings, we introduce the RealWorld-to-Verifiable Construction Framework, which transforms real-world developer queries and historical evidence into verifiable evaluation tasks. We evaluate 15 coding agents on 1,661 cases from 65 GitHub repositories. Within Claude Code, Claude Opus 4.8 achieves the highest SWE-Time Avg. of 61.9, leaving substantial headroom. Controlled analyses highlight the importance of historical code evidence and developer intent, while consistent reasoning across repository states remains challenging. These results highlight repository evolution as a distinct and challenging dimension of code understanding.

title: Toward Sustainable Agentic AI: Carbon Tradeoffs Across Iterative Self-Refinement and Tool-Augmented Coding
abstract: Agentic language model systems can improve performance either by iterating on their own outputs or by using external tools in grounded environments. While these strategies can reduce error rates and substitute for larger models in some settings, their environmental cost remains relatively underexplored. We present two complementary empirical studies that estimate the energy and carbon footprint of agentic AI across settings of increasing complexity. Study~1 evaluates iterative verbal self-refinement: GPT-4.1-mini at $k = 1$--$5$ steps versus a GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline on two MATH benchmark splits. Study~2 evaluates tool-augmented agentic coding: GPT-4.1-mini, Claude Opus~4.6, and GPT-5.3-codex on SWE-bench Lite, where agents operate inside Docker-isolated environments with access to code execution and file editing tools. In Study~1, $k=3$ refinements close a 16-percentage-point accuracy gap to within 1~point, but nearly triple the carbon footprint relative to the cheap single-pass baseline while remaining below the GPT-4.1 single-pass baseline under the current token-based carbon scenario. In Study~2, GPT-5.3-codex achieves the highest resolution rate in this sample (81.2\%), ahead of Claude Opus~4.6 (68.9\%) and GPT-4.1-mini (25.0\%), but resolved-task-normalized efficiency remains mixed: GPT-4.1-mini is lowest on estimated carbon and cost per resolved task, while GPT-5.3-codex delivers substantially higher task success. All carbon estimates cover output-token inference only; prompt tokens, which exceed 99\% of tokens in Study~2, and tool execution are not charged, so the figures are lower bounds on the full agentic footprint.

title: Unmasking shortcut solutions of coding agents on partial differential equations
abstract: Coding agents now write simulation programs, but benchmarks usually judge only whether their output matches a reference. In manufactured-solution tasks the data determine the exact solution, so a matching output need not come from a solver. We introduce PDEViBench, a benchmark of 290 tasks in six equation families that traces each passing program to the computation behind its output and reruns unclear programs on changed data. A Codex agent (GPT-5.2) passed 80% of 1,450 runs, yet about one pass in ten returned the exact solution without solving the equation. Counting only solved passes changed which task features made problems seem hard and reversed the ranking of two prompts. Once the prompt forbade the shortcut, every pass was a numerical solve, and on tasks without a closed-form solution passing programs stayed correct on changed data. Scientific coding benchmarks should check how each answer was computed as well as whether it matches.

title: SHADOWPREFILL: Keeping Your Next Model Warm for Per-Step Model Routing in Agentic LLM Serving
abstract: Per-step model routers send each LLM call of an agent to the cost-optimal model dynamically within each session. However, every model switch discards prefix-cache reuse: KV caches are per model, so the new model must prefill the relevant context before it emits a token. Across representative agentic workloads, including a production coding-agent trace with a mean context of 63K tokens, the prefix hit rate falls from 80-89% on same model calls to 44-65% after a switch, and a switch call takes 1.5-3.2x as long. We present SHADOWPREFILL, which prefills the session's context on the model the router has not chosen, in capacity that instances serving normal traffic leave idle, so the next switch finds its prefix cached. SHADOWPREFILL harvests the per-iteration SLO slack of requests in flight, protects routed calls, spills shadow KV to host memory, and falls back to a cold switch whenever the shadow is incomplete. With LLMRouter routing 24 model pairs over five agentic benchmark suites, SHADOWPREFILL cuts switch-call latency by 8.5-21.4%, LLM-call latency by 3.7-17.7%, and routed token cost by 22.5-46.1%, while normal traffic keeps its SLO and energy per request rises by 0.4%.

title: FlowPlan: Reducing the Token Cost of Coding Agents with Abstraction-Guided Planning and Verification
abstract: LLM-based coding agents such as Claude Code can resolve real-world repository issues, but their iterative interaction loop can be expensive. Existing approaches reduce this cost primarily by limiting, compressing, or selectively avoiding information and actions within the repair process. We investigate a complementary question: Can an agent reason about a repair at an abstract program level, rather than repeatedly operating over raw source code, to reduce both the exploration needed to identify a repair and the repeated checking needed to verify it afterward? We present FlowPlan, an abstraction-guided repair approach that structures localization, planning, and verification around per-function control-flow or data-flow graphs. The agent first localizes the candidate fault location on the program abstraction and expresses the intended repair as explicit graph deltas before modifying the concrete source. After the edit, FlowPlan reconstructs the same abstraction and compares the observed structural change with the planned one. Then, a verification checks the complete repair before termination. Across all six benchmark-model settings, FlowPlan does not significantly change resolution rate relative to the vanilla agent while reducing token consumption in every setting, significantly in five of six settings. With Claude Haiku 4.5, it uses only 0.46-0.47x the baseline tokens on SWE-bench Pro, 0.32-0.35x on SWE-bench Verified, and 0.68-0.74x on SecBench; with Sonnet 5, it uses 0.72-0.76x, 0.73-0.74x, and 0.92-0.94x, respectively. Overall, FlowPlan achieves the largest token reduction among the compared methods in three of the six settings and ties the strongest compared method in a fourth. Trajectory analysis shows that FlowPlan saves tokens by replacing much of the costly post-edit re-reading and testing with explicit verification and reducing per-call context.

title: ExpertCrowd-SWE: Measuring Frontier Coding Agents on Expert-Authored Engineering Tasks in Unfamiliar Codebases
abstract: ExpertCrowd-SWE (EC-SWE) is a benchmark of 100 expert-authored, multi-file software engineering tasks for evaluating autonomous coding agents in large, unfamiliar codebases. Each task is a change request written by a practising engineer against a pinned commit of a real repository, paired with a sealed reference solution and a task-specific grader whose weighted, mostly executable criteria award partial credit; must-pass blockers and pass/fail gates encode what a maintainer would refuse to merge. The tasks span 87 open-source projects and 11 languages. The median ticket is 148 words, while the median reference solution changes 471 lines. Every task image is calibrated before release so that the reference solution scores 1.0 and both the untouched repository and an inert change score 0; nearly half of the tasks also ship alternative, lazy and adversarial control patches that the grader must classify correctly. The final 100 tasks were selected for difficulty against current frontier models. We evaluate seven frontier models, five runs each (3,495 scored runs), in a single platform harness that gives each model its provider-native tool interface. Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3%) and GPT-6 Astra (63.7%) lead without a statistically significant gap, followed by Claude Fable 5.1 (46.5%), Gemini 3.8 Flash (40.0%), and a statistically indistinguishable group of Qwen 3.8 Max, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Grok 4.6 (32-34%). No task is fully solved by every model, and on 80 tasks no model earns full credit on all five runs. Scores span 35 points. Depending on the model, agents take a median of 33 to 166 steps per run, with little relation to score. We release 24 tasks with their environments, graders and results, and hold out 76 to limit contamination.

title: The AI Era's Lines of Code? A Case Study on What an Engineer's Token Spend Measures
abstract: Organizations use engineers' token spend to monitor AI adoption, set budgets, and measure productivity, but the metric's relationship with engineering output is unclear. We link five weeks of token usage in coding agents to the commits of 404 engineers at JetBrains, and analyze a company survey of 412 employees. We find that token spend varied mostly between engineers, and which engineers spent the most stayed largely the same over the five weeks. Among weeks with similar commit counts, the 90th percentile of spend was 39 to 240 times the 10th. Within an engineer, doubling spend was associated with about 10% more commits. Available work metrics explained 38% of the variation in spend between engineers and 13% of the week-to-week variation within an engineer. In the survey, respondents in technical roles reported in nearly nine of ten agent evaluations using agents for tasks beyond coding, such as analysis, research, and planning. Token spend therefore measures how much engineers use agents across many kinds of work and not the outcome and value of that work. We recommend using token spend at most for resource accounting, and evaluating agent-assisted work with evidence about tasks and outcomes.

title: BioXArena-Pro: a research-grade benchmark for autonomous biomedical machine learning agents
abstract: Coding agents are increasingly proposed as autonomous builders of biomedical models, but existing benchmarks are small, near saturation or open to leaked information. We present BioXArena-Pro, 64 research-level modelling tasks from eight biomedical domains, each rebuilt from a published study; most hold out whole biological units such as species or cohorts. Across 22 agent configurations, the best scores 55.1 of 100, and the scaffold matters almost as much as the model. We re-ran a published method for every task: where the published recipe applies unchanged, the best agent and the methods tie; on rebuilt tasks the methods trail by 8.2 points, suggesting that agents gain by adapting to new data. Pretrained models (including biological foundation models) matter where the strongest agent uses them: forbidding them decreases its score on those tasks by 9 points. Every task was audited in several AI-assisted rounds and a final human review.

title: Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II: Unlocking the Memory Potential of Pre-trained File Operations for Long-Horizon Tasks via On-Policy Distillation
abstract: Language-model agents increasingly tackle long-horizon tasks whose interaction histories exceed the model's active context. They must therefore decide what to write down and what to read back, and when to do either. Recent work has begun to use on-policy distillation (OPD) to make memory control part of the policy, relying on memory tools and compaction protocols that lie outside either model's pre-training. However, this weakens the distillation on both sides: the teacher cannot give useful guidance on an interface it has never used, and the student samples too few meaningful memory actions for that guidance to take effect. To study this problem, we introduce Coding Agent Memory Gym II (CAMG-II), a suite of long-horizon agentic-RL environments spanning Shop, Coding, AutoResearch, General, and Visual. Alongside each environment's native task interface, CAMG-II provides ordinary Bash access and an episode-persistent workspace, enabling the policy to create, revise, search, and reuse files as memory across context replacements. We also introduce Coding Agent Memory Post-Training II (CAMP-II), which trains a single policy jointly across all five environments with fully asynchronous OPD to learn this file-based memory behavior directly from a frozen teacher with a prior for file operations. On CAMG-II, CAMP-II obtains 2.97 times the gain of the strongest OPD baseline. The memory behavior CAMP-II learns generalizes to two external benchmarks, Terminal-Bench 2.1 and SWE-Bench Pro V2, with improved success rates.

title: ProofCoder: Continuous Reasoning for Automated Software Verification
abstract: Formal verification using proof assistants provides strong correctness guarantees for software, but constructing proofs remains labor-intensive and requires significant expertise. Recent approaches based on large language models (LLMs) have shown promise in automating proof synthesis. However, these approaches typically constrain the model to a rigid tactic-generation loop, in which the surrounding system controls premise retrieval, proof-state management, and backtracking. We introduce ProofCoder, an agentic proof-synthesis system for Rocq that approaches theorem proving from a coding-agent perspective. Rather than generating tactics within a fixed loop, ProofCoder reasons continuously throughout proof search and uses proof-assistant feedback to decide when to gather additional information, inspect proof states, revise previously generated proof fragments, or backtrack to an earlier point in the proof. This allows it to iteratively construct, repair, and refine proofs, at either tactic-level or whole-proof granularity. We evaluate ProofCoder on 280 challenging verification tasks from the AutoRocq Benchmark. On the best-performing configurations, ProofCoder increases proof success from 47% to 60% over the state-of-theart AutoRocq system, corresponding to a 27.7% relative improvement at approximately half the cost. Our ablations identify continuous reasoning as a key design choice: without it, the agent solves fewer lemmas at substantially higher cost, backtracks four to six times more often, and more frequently discards its own revisions. Whole-proof and tactic-level generation achieve similar success rates but follow distinct search and repair strategies. These results suggest that effective automated software verification requires more than improved tactic selection: continuous reasoning and feedback-guided proof revision are critical ingredients for robust proof synthesis.

title: EngineAgent: Agentizing On-Device LLM Inference Engines with Inference Stack Hierarchy Awareness and Hardware Abilities
abstract: Rapidly evolving LLM architectures and heterogeneous mobile hardware make supporting new models in on-device inference engines a recurring and costly system challenge. Each model may require coordinated changes across conversion, graph construction, operators, and hardware backends. Existing coding agents often miss these cross-layer dependencies and struggle to diagnose failures across host--device execution paths. We present EngineAgent, an agentic system for automating on-device LLM model enablement. Its key insight is to separate reusable engine and hardware knowledge from model-specific implementation. Before enablement, EngineAgent constructs a hierarchy-aware engine index that captures engine abstraction layers and cross-layer dependencies, and pre-validates backend-specific build, execution, and debugging workflows using already supported models. For each new model, a builder uses this knowledge to coordinate cross-layer changes, while an auditor checks implementation completeness and drives iterative debugging through device-side validation. Across 12 tasks spanning three mobile LLMs and four engine--backend pairs on CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, EngineAgent achieves 75% end-to-end success with either of two underlying LLMs, versus 33.3% for the strongest coding-agent baseline. Success requires compilation, on-device execution, and output-logit agreement with reference implementations. EngineAgent also reduces average per-task time and model-API cost relative to baselines using the same underlying LLMs.

title: One Policy for 100 Household Tasks: Our Solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge
abstract: We describe our solution for the 2026 BEHAVIOR Challenge: 100 long-horizon household tasks in the OmniGibson simulator. We placed 9th on the final leaderboard, the only independent team in the top 10. The core of the solution is a single vision-language-action (VLA) model, one checkpoint for all 100 tasks, built on our 1st-place 2025 solution, which is based on $π_{0.5}$. On the 50 tasks shared with 2025, its Q rises from 0.260 to 0.371; across all 100 tasks it scores 0.392. Our main conclusion from 2025 was that the model was undertrained, so most of the 2026 work went into training the model for longer, optimizing some training parameters, making each training step slightly faster and reducing the gradient noise: a migration from 50 to 100 tasks (semantic stages built from the demonstrations' skill annotations, task and stage embeddings of new tasks warm-started from similar old ones, and a 21-dimensional action space matching the teleoperation controls); variance-reduced multi-sample flow matching with a simple noise-vs-compute model that picks the number of action-expert samples per observation without ablations; and a 200k-step training run, about one pass over the 211M frames of the demonstrations. A cloud evaluation infrastructure keeps a shared record with provenance, episode diagnostics and restorable simulator states, and runs six simulators on one GPU together faster than real time. On top of the learned policy, 14 tasks are routed to a GPT-6 Astra coding agent that controls the robot through observation and motion tools, starting every episode from a frozen copy of its own practice session on training instances. Across these 14 tasks, Astra's mean Q is 0.639, against 0.108 for the learned policy. The public submission included only part of the Astra results and scored 0.446 Q with 27.3% full-task success.

title: JoyFrontBench: Evaluating Front-End Coding Agents through Goal-Oriented Acceptance Contracts
abstract: Front-end coding agents are expected to produce applications that fulfill user goals, yet high task scores can coexist with failures in essential workflows. Evaluating these agents therefore requires an explicit distinction between partial implementation and application success. We introduce JoyFrontBench, a benchmark that makes this distinction through goal-oriented acceptance contracts. Each contract identifies core tasks and mandatory criteria before generation: a core task passes only when all mandatory criteria are satisfied and a shared completion threshold is met, while application success requires every core task to pass on the same operational artifact within a single run. Derived from practitioner requirements, JoyFrontBench comprises 100 front-end development problems, 764 tasks, and 2,596 atomic criteria, with reviewed annotations linking user goals to core tasks and evidence requirements. The evaluation framework combines evidence-grounded judgments with deterministic record auditing and fixed scoring rules, preserving graded task assessment alongside explicit core-task and application-level acceptance. We evaluate five coding models under two agent harnesses, OpenHands and OpenCode, on the 70-problem test set; the remaining 30 problems form a public set for validation and diagnostic analyses. Under OpenHands, the mean Average Task Score (ATS) across models is 87.69%, while the mean Application Success Rate (ASR) is 51.52%. Further analyses reveal changes in model rankings across harnesses and variation in application success across repeated runs. These findings highlight the limitations of aggregate task scores in characterizing application success and motivate explicit assessment of core-goal fulfillment alongside graded task performance.

title: WordInferBench: Can Agents Infer How to Edit from Word Document Context?
abstract: Document editing is among the most common knowledge-work tasks, yet existing benchmarks for evaluating autonomous agents on Word document editing provide fully specified attribute-modification instructions. They do not evaluate agents' ability to infer the appropriate attributes from document context, a capability essential in real-world editing where users expect consistency without spelling out every attribute. We introduce WordInferBench, a benchmark comprising 280 base document-editing instances, each paired with three instruction conditions: descriptive (the instruction explicitly lists every attribute change), referential (the instruction points to another object as an exemplar), and inferential (the agent must examine document context to infer what attributes to apply). To evaluate contextual attribute inference, each base instance is constructed so that the target formatting is recoverable from an in-document exemplar. The instances are derived from real Word documents collected from Common Crawl and cover 13 object types and 81 attributes. We evaluate six recent coding-agent systems and find that the best-performing evaluated system, Claude Code with Opus 4.6, achieves a 62.9% task-level pass rate on descriptive variants but only 40.7% on inferential variants, indicating that current systems complete tasks less reliably when the required formatting changes must be determined from document context.

title: Where Autonomy Belongs: A Separation of Powers for Agentic Program Evolution
abstract: LLM-driven program evolution rests on three decisions: govern directs the search from accumulated evidence, propose constructs the next candidate, and judge settles validity and fitness. All three appear in every system, and existing work splits into two lines over who makes each. Controller-centric systems strengthen govern and neglect the autonomy of propose, which caps what evolution can reach. Agent-centric systems let a coding agent take over both govern and propose, at a cognitive and computational cost. Neither line protects the independent authority of judge, so benchmark reliability suffers. These failures share one root: autonomy is misallocated across the three decisions. We address this problem with EvoTrias, a separation-of-powers architecture in which each decision has one owner: Structured Governance for what spans evolution rounds, Open Proposal for construction inside a task, and Protected Judgment behind a private evaluator. These owners exchange typed contracts only, and runtime hooks reinforce the boundaries. This separation also lets EvoTrias run as a plugin that turns an existing coding agent into an evolution system. EvoTrias sets a new state of the art on mathematical, systems, and algorithm-design benchmarks. Three further results show what each owner buys: separating Governance from Proposal cuts token cost by 64%, Open Proposal extends evolution to a 680K-line industrial repository, and Protected Judgment keeps benchmark scores faithful to transfer.

title: Technical Debt Risks in AI-Assisted Software Development: Insights from Practitioners
abstract: AI coding assistants increasingly support software development, raising concerns about technical debt associated with AI-generated code and development practices. We investigate these concerns through a sequential mixed-methods study involving 137 survey respondents and 20 follow-up interviews with software professionals in Bangladesh. Drawing on ten established technical debt dimensions, we examine perceived risks, contributing circumstances, maintenance consequences, validation practices, and developer understanding. Respondents expressed the strongest concerns about People Debt (73.0\%), Management Debt (70.1\%), and Architecture Debt (68.6\%), suggesting that risks extend beyond code quality. Participants associated ambiguous requirements, insufficient project context, and unrequested AI-generated changes with architectural inconsistencies, rework, and maintenance difficulties. Their experiences revealed contrasting outcomes: AI assistance supported refactoring, maintainability improvements, and testing, but also introduced rework and context misalignment. Although 89.8\% reported regularly verifying AI-generated code, participants expressed concerns about AI dependence, reduced code understanding, and review effort. They also emphasized the need for stronger architectural awareness, requirements clarification, and validation support in coding assistants. Our findings suggest that managing technical debt risks requires attention to project context, implementation decisions, and developer understanding alongside generated code quality.

title: Bug Finding With Agentic Symbolic Execution
abstract: Symbolic execution, in tools such as CrossHair for Python, is a powerful technique for finding bugs, but two barriers hinder its adoption: the human effort of annotating code with assertions, and the need to model the execution environment outside Python, such as an external database. To overcome both, we design an agentic harness that orchestrates the symbolic execution tool CrossHair together with an AI coding agent. Without human intervention, it instruments a repository with assertions, synthesizes a constraint-aware symbolic environment for the database, runs symbolic execution, and constructs a concrete test as evidence for each bug it reports. We evaluate our harness on 1,156,044 lines of Python code over 11 popular open-source Python web applications (Zulip, NetBox, Apache Superset, and others). With the synthesized environment, CrossHair executes 81% of the 5,406 contracted functions, against 4.5% without it. Our pipeline finds 1,050 bugs, each reproduced by a test against the unmodified application, 221 of them by CrossHair, and 312 of them are missed by a baseline in which the same LLM inspects the code. The two find different kinds of bugs: CrossHair's are mostly crashes on input-domain corner cases that validation admits, such as empty strings, missing fields and unusual characters, while inspection's are mostly bugs that produce wrong output. Our framework thus lets symbolic execution supplement inspection-based bug finding.

title: What World Model Does Active Object Search Need? A Study under Imperfect Detection
abstract: In active object search, a robot must decide where to look and when to stop. Imperfect detection complicates both decisions: a non-detection may indicate occlusion, an out-of-view target, or a false negative, while a detection may be a false positive. This raises the question of which representations a world model needs to support reliable search under imperfect detection. We introduce Bayesian Active Miss-aware Object Search (BAMOS) to investigate how target belief, occupancy belief, and detector errors affect search decisions.
